analysis.one_liner: Shifts $6.5 billion from the bank bailout fund to foreclosure relief and affordable housing.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have redirected $6.5 billion in bank bailout money to homeowners and neighborhoods, got one committee hearing and never came up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken $6.5 billion from the Troubled Asset Relief Program — the 2008 bank bailout — and spent it on people losing their homes instead. It would have sent $1 billion to a national affordable-housing fund, $1.5 billion to fix up abandoned and foreclosed houses, $2 billion to an emergency fund that helps homeowners behind on mortgages after job losses, and $2 billion to stabilize apartment buildings falling into default, with protections for their tenants. To cover the cost, it would have cut the bailout program's remaining size.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners behind on their mortgages after a job loss or income drop, renters in apartment buildings slipping into foreclosure, and neighborhoods with abandoned, foreclosed houses that drag down nearby property values. The money would have flowed to state and local governments and to HUD programs rather than to individuals directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: At-risk homeowners, renters, and foreclosed neighborhoods

how_it_helps.text: Transfers $1 billion from TARP bank dividends to the Housing Trust Fund, which builds and preserves affordable rental housing for low-income families.
Sends $1.5 billion to state and local governments to redevelop abandoned and foreclosed homes under the Neighborhood Stabilization Program formula, with the money available until spent.
Moves $2 billion into an Emergency Homeowners' Relief Fund for emergency mortgage assistance, and extends and enlarges that program through fiscal year 2011.

Provides $2 billion to stabilize apartment buildings with five or more units that are in default or foreclosure, including financing, rehabilitation funds, and protections for current and future tenants.
Offsets the cost by reducing the TARP authorization limit, so the relief is paid for out of the existing bailout program rather than new borrowing.

analysis.who_pays: Banks that received TARP assistance, whose dividend money and share of the bailout program's remaining authorization would have been redirected to housing relief. To the extent those funds would otherwise have been returned or used to shrink the bailout, the Treasury forgoes them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks that received TARP bailout funds

drawbacks.text: The bill draws down the same TARP pool that backs the effort to stabilize the banking system, and cuts the program's remaining authorization by the cost of the new loans, advances, insurance, and appropriations — a trade-off an honest supporter had to acknowledge: less cushion for bank stabilization.

Emergency mortgage assistance programs help homeowners catch up on arrears but cannot restore the lost income that caused the default; borrowers who remain unemployed after the assistance runs out can still lose the home, so the relief may delay rather than prevent some foreclosures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was self-financing within the existing bailout program, using dividends from banks the government had already rescued, so it asked taxpayers for no new money. The main cost was opportunity: every dollar redirected to homeowners and neighborhoods was a dollar no longer available for bank stabilization or deficit reduction. Given that the bailout money had come from taxpayers in the first place, steering a slice of it to the people actually losing homes was a modest rebalancing, and the bill's scale — about $6.5 billion in a program of roughly $700 billion — was small relative to the problem.

outcome.mechanism: The chairman of the Financial Services Committee introduced it, the committee held one hearing in July 2009, and then it sat with no markup and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Barney Frank of Massachusetts, chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on June 26, 2009 with Maxine Waters, Dennis Cardoza, and Nydia Velázquez as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which held a hearing on July 9, 2009.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's final recorded action was that July 2009 hearing, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks that received TARP bailout money, and the bailout program itself, kept the $6.5 billion the bill would have redirected. Homeowners facing foreclosure and neighborhoods with abandoned properties got nothing from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and chaired the committee that held its only hearing.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on July 9, 2009 and then took no further action; never reported the bill for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were House Democrats, including the committee chairman; no House Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a roll-call vote.

industries.industry: Banks that received TARP bailout funds
industries.note: The bill would have redirected $1 billion in TARP dividends and transferred another $5.5 billion from bailout authority, while cutting the program's remaining authorization to cover costs. Bank bailout money staying in the financial rescue instead of flowing to foreclosure relief is the direct cost to this group.

The bill would have provided $2 billion in sustainable financing, rehabilitation funds, and facilitated transfers for multifamily properties in default or foreclosure. Owners would have gained a way out of default, but only under conditions protecting tenants and maintaining subsidies.
The $1.5 billion for redeveloping abandoned and foreclosed homes would have funded local demolition, repair, and resale work in hard-hit neighborhoods.
